paragraphs.heading: A civilization on the Nile
paragraphs.text: Ancient Egypt was a cradle of civilization that grew up along the lower Nile River in the eastern part of North Africa. By the usual chronology it took shape around 3150 BC, when Upper and Lower Egypt were joined under Menes. Most Egyptologists think Menes was the same person as Narmer. Its history then ran as a series of stable kingdoms, broken up by Intermediate Periods of relative unrest. Those stable stretches are the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms.

paragraphs.heading: Empire and decline
paragraphs.text: Egypt was at its most powerful in the New Kingdom, also called the Egyptian Empire, when it ruled much of Nubia and a large part of the Levant. After that came a slow decline. Over the centuries Egypt was invaded or conquered by many foreign peoples, among them the Hyksos, Kushites, Assyrians, Persians, Greeks and Romans. Historians date its end either to Alexander the Great's wars in 332 BC or to the Roman conquest in 30 BC.

paragraphs.heading: Why the river mattered
paragraphs.text: Egypt succeeded partly because it adapted farming to the Nile's conditions. The river flooded on a regular schedule, and people channelled its water across the fertile valley. This produced extra food, which fed a denser population and allowed rich social and cultural growth. The Nile's floodplain made a settled farming economy possible, and with it a more complex, centralized society.

paragraphs.heading: Running a kingdom
paragraphs.text: With spare resources, the government paid for mining in the valley and the deserts around it, an early writing system of its own, group building and farming projects, foreign trade, and an army. A class of elite scribes, priests and officials organized all this under the reigning pharaoh. The pharaoh kept the people united and cooperating within a detailed system of religious beliefs.

paragraphs.heading: Before the pharaohs
paragraphs.text: In early times Egypt was much less dry than today, and large parts were savanna crossed by herds of grazing animals. Plants and wildlife were far richer, and the Nile region held huge numbers of waterbirds. By about 5500 BC, small tribes in the valley had become cultures that farmed and herded with confidence. The largest of these in the south was the Badarian culture, known for fine pottery, stone tools and the use of copper.

paragraphs.heading: The Naqada culture
paragraphs.text: The Badarian was followed by the Naqada culture, which over about 1,000 years grew from a few small farming villages into a strong civilization whose leaders controlled the whole Nile valley. Its people brought obsidian from Ethiopia to make blades and began trading with the Levant and Mesopotamia. Ruling first from Nekhen and later from Abydos, Naqada leaders pushed their control northwards. They also made faience, a ceramic glaze for cups, amulets and figurines. In their last phase they began using written symbols that later grew into hieroglyphs.

paragraphs.heading: Menes and unification
paragraphs.text: Manetho, an Egyptian priest of the third century BC, sorted the kings from Menes to his own day into 30 dynasties, a scheme still in use. He began his history with Menes, who was believed to have united Upper and Lower Egypt. In truth unification happened more slowly than Egyptian writers claimed, and no record of Menes from his own time exists. Some scholars think he may have been King Narmer, shown in royal dress on the Narmer Palette in a symbolic act of uniting the land. Around 3000 BC the first kings set up a capital at Memphis to control the fertile delta and its trade routes to the Levant.

paragraphs.heading: The Old Kingdom
paragraphs.text: The Old Kingdom saw big steps forward in building, art and technology, driven by better harvests and a growing population under a strong central government. The Giza pyramids and the Great Sphinx were built in this period. Led by the vizier, officials gathered taxes, organized irrigation to raise crop yields and called up peasants to work on building projects. A new class of educated scribes and officials appeared, and the king paid them with estates.
